attractions.summary: All checked dates, names, dimensions and the tongue legend match Wikipedia, the Adam Clark article and budapest.com; coordinates match OSM.

claims.claim: Opened 20 November 1849; first permanent bridge across the Danube in Hungary
claims.note: Wikipedia: opened 20 Nov 1849, 'the first permanent bridge across the Danube in Hungary'; budapest.com gives the same opening date.

claims.claim: Designed 1839 by English engineer William Tierney Clark; Scottish engineer Adam Clark supervised construction 1840-1849, no relation
claims.note: Both Wikipedia articles: design 1839, Adam Clark Scottish, 'no relation'.

claims.claim: Total length about 375 m, width 14.8 m, centre span 202 m, one of the largest in the world at the time
claims.note: 375 m, 202 m span, 'one of the largest suspension bridges in the world at the time'; Wikipedia gives 14.8 m width.

claims.claim: Wrought iron and stone, cast-iron decoration
claims.note: Infobox 'Wrought iron and stone'; decorations 'made of cast iron'.

claims.claim: Georgios Sinas funded much of it; name inscribed on base of south-western foundation, Buda side
claims.note: Matches Wikipedia wording.

claims.claim: 1848: Clark helped Kossuth's army cross, one estimate 70,000 men and 300 guns in a day; early 1849 flooded anchorage chambers, only one of four gunpowder canisters detonated; June 1849 persuaded Henryk Dembinski not to destroy whole bridge, platform dismantled
claims.note: All present; the 70,000 figure is presented as 'one estimate', as the dossier words it.

claims.claim: Marschalkó lions installed 1852; present name 1898; strengthened 1914
claims.note: Matches.

claims.claim: Blown up by retreating German forces 18 January 1945, only towers left; rebuilt, reopened 1949
claims.note: 18 Jan 1945, only stone towers survived, reopened 20 Nov 1949; Wikipedia 'only the towers remaining'.

claims.claim: Lions-have-no-tongues story is untrue; tongues just not visible from below
claims.note: Wikipedia calls the legend untrue; budapest.com says tongues are visible only from above at close range. Tip wording ('said to be there') is acceptable.

claims.claim: Adam Clark Square renamed 1912; contains Zero Kilometre Stone; funicular starts there
claims.note: 1912 renaming and Zero Kilometre Stone confirmed; Chain Bridge article places funicular lower end at the square.

claims.claim: Buda Castle Tunnel commissioned by the Hungarian government in 1850, opened to foot traffic March 1856
claims.note: Foot traffic March 1856 confirmed on the page; the 1850 government commission appears in the Wikipedia article per search excerpt (a Hungarian source questions who drew the original plan, which the dossier does not claim). Vehicle opening 1857 per budapest.com.
OSM bridge at 47.49898, 19.04365; within ~15 m.

claims.claim: Dome reached by lift or 364 steps

claims.note: WWII damage, 1947 fire, 1982 storm, restoration 1983-2003.

attractions.summary: Core dates and coronations check out, but the tower attribution, the crypt museum wording and the 1309 crown story were not supported as written and were corrected.

claims.claim: Béla IV, 1255-1269, replaced older church with three-nave basilica
claims.note: Matches.

claims.claim: Tradition of Stephen's foundation in 1015, no clear evidence
claims.note: Church tradition based on 1690 inscription; 'no clear evidence'.

claims.claim: Matthias Corvinus built the south-west bell tower; married here 1463 and 1476
claims.note: Weddings confirmed (also on official chronology). But the tower collapsed in 1384 and, per Matthias's coat of arms, was rebuilt in 1470; the official chronology only mentions the coat of arms, and Schulek later rebuilt the cap. 'Built' overstated.

claims.claim: Franz Joseph and Elisabeth crowned 1867 with Liszt's Coronation Mass premiere
claims.note: 8 June 1867; Wikipedia confirms Liszt Mass first performed.

claims.claim: Charles IV and Zita crowned 30 December 1916; Charles IV last king
claims.note: 'coronation of the last king of Hungary'.

claims.claim: Mosque 1541 to 1686; Jesuits restored it in Baroque style
claims.note: Matches Wikipedia; official chronology confirms conversion in 1541 and reconquest 1686.

claims.claim: Schulek restoration 1874-1896 gave steep Gothic spire and gargoyles
claims.note: Wikipedia 1874-1896 (official chronology says started 1873, consecrated 1896); neo-Gothic cap, 'gargoyles laden spire'.

claims.claim: Murals by Székely and Lotz, stained glass designed by them
claims.note: They painted murals and designed the windows (executed by Kratzmann).

claims.claim: Medieval crypt houses the Ecclesiastical Art Museum
claims.note: Official chronology: museum established in the church in 1964, no crypt mention; Wikipedia says it 'begins in the medieval crypt' but also says the crypt dates from 1780 and was renewed. Reworded.

claims.claim: 1309 Charles I crowned with a provisional crown; later coronation with the Holy Crown
claims.note: Church chronology says 'provisional crown' in 1309; Wikipedia says a newly consecrated crown was used in 1309 (the provisional crown was 1301) and the Holy Crown coronation was at Székesfehérvár on 27 Aug 1310. The church page does not state the later Holy Crown coronation, so the attribution was wrong.

claims.claim: Church of Our Lady under construction mid-13th century; reconquest 1686 returned it to Christian worship; WWII damage and restoration
claims.note: Damage in 1944-45 siege, restoration from 1954 into the 1970s.

claims.claim: Address Szentháromság tér 2; coordinates 47.50200, 19.03416
claims.note: Wikipedia 47.50194, 19.03417; essentially identical.

corrections.find: who built the south-west bell tower, one of the finest pieces of Gothic architecture in Hungary, and who married here in 1463 and 1476
corrections.replace: whose coat of arms on the south-west bell tower dates its rebuilding to 1470 (the earlier tower had collapsed in 1384), and who married here in 1463 and 1476
corrections.reason: Sources say the south tower collapsed in 1384 and was rebuilt in 1470 according to Matthias's coat of arms; the official chronology only mentions the coat of arms, so 'built' overstates his role.

corrections.find: The medieval crypt houses the Ecclesiastical Art Museum
corrections.replace: The Ecclesiastical Art Museum begins in the crypt
corrections.reason: Wikipedia says the museum begins in the crypt but notes the crypt dates from 1780 and was renewed in neo-Gothic style; the official chronology says only that the museum was set up in the church in 1964. 'Medieval crypt' is unsupported.

corrections.find: In 1309 Charles I was crowned in the church with a provisional crown. The church's own historical account notes that his kingship required a later coronation with the Holy Crown of Hungary.
corrections.replace: In 1309 Charles I was crowned in the church; the church's own chronology calls the crown provisional, while other sources describe a newly consecrated crown. His coronation with the Holy Crown of Hungary followed at Székesfehérvár in 1310.
corrections.reason: The official chronology says 'provisional crown' in 1309 but does not mention a later Holy Crown coronation; Wikipedia says a new crown was used in 1309 and the Holy Crown coronation was in Székesfehérvár on 27 August 1310. Sources differ on the 1309 crown, so this is qualified.

sourceIssues.issue: Does not state the later Holy Crown coronation, does not mention Béla IV's 1255-1269 rebuild, and does not place the museum in a crypt; the history story attributed to it overstated its content.
Not checked; budapestinfo.hu pages returned only titles in this check.

attractions.summary: Medieval and 19th-century palace history verified; the 1952-1966 reconstruction dates and 'medieval fortifications rebuilt' were unsupported and reworded. Phase 18: The claim that the district 'grew around the royal residence' was not supported and is actually backwards: the Academy's Buda history page says the fortified town was founded first and the royal court was later accommodated in the growing town. The sentence now says the district began as a walled town founded by Béla IV.

claims.claim: First royal residence built 1247-1265 under Béla IV
claims.note: 'built by King Béla IV between 1247 and 1265' (location uncertain).

claims.claim: Sigismund extended it 1410s-1420s; Matthias rebuilt it in early Renaissance style after 1476 marriage to Beatrice
claims.note: Matches.

claims.claim: Buda fell to Ottomans in 1541; 1686 siege destroyed medieval palace
claims.note: Ottoman occupation 29 Aug 1541; 'destroyed in the great siege of 1686'.

claims.claim: Small Baroque palace in 18th century, enlarged under Maria Theresa, finished 1769
claims.note: 1715 small Baroque palace (Hölbling); new palace begun 1749, finished 1769.

claims.claim: Rebuilt after 1849 siege fires to designs associated with Ybl and Hauszmann; inaugurated 1912
claims.note: Rebuilding 1875-1912; Ybl died 1891, Hauszmann succeeded; 'officially inaugurated in 1912'.

claims.claim: 1944-45 siege left palace in ruins; reconstruction 1952-1966 in simplified Baroque style; medieval fortifications rebuilt
claims.note: Wikipedia: palace rebuilt by 1966, interiors only ready in the 1980s, modernist dome 1961. No source seen for a 1952 start or for 'medieval fortifications rebuilt'; search results mention medieval rooms unearthed and reconstructed 1958-62.

claims.claim: Palace houses Hungarian National Gallery, Budapest History Museum, National Széchényi Library
claims.note: Named in the lead.

claims.claim: UNESCO listing 'Budapest, including the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue', inscribed 1987
claims.note: Castle Quarter within the area inscribed in 1987.

claims.claim: Funicular climbs from Clark Ádám tér beside the Chain Bridge
claims.note: Matches.

claims.claim: Castle District grew around medieval royal residence; courtyards, lanes, churches, viewpoints
claims.note: Courtyards, streets, churches and viewpoints supported; 'grew around the royal residence' is general and not stated verbatim.

resolution.note: Hungarian Academy of Sciences Buda history page: Béla IV had a fortress built on Castle Hill after the Mongol invasion, curtain walls enclosed the plateau, and 'After its foundation the growing town and the strong fortification soon accommodated the royal court as well.' So the town preceded the court; Wikipedia (Várhegy) agrees: Béla IV built the first fort 1247-1265 after the Mongol invasion, surrounded the settlement with walls, and the neighbourhood grew with Hungarians and Germans and the first royal palace was built. Courtyards, lanes, churches and viewpoints remain as stated (Visit Budavár lists churches, palace courtyards, viewpoints).

claims.claim: Address Szent György tér 2; coordinates 47.49646, 19.03987
claims.note: Wikipedia 47.4961, 19.0397; within ~40 m. Address is the palace address; the district covers a wider area.

claims.claim: Coordinates 47.49646, 19.03987 (palace / Szent György tér 2)
claims.note: Wikipedia gives the palace at 47.49611, 19.03972, about 40 m from the site point. Address Szent György tér 2, 1014 matches the address Budapest.com gives for the palace.

claims.claim: Palace houses the Hungarian National Gallery, Budapest History Museum and National Széchényi Library
claims.note: Visit Budavár lists the three institutions in the former royal palace.

claims.claim: Matthias Fountain in the western forecourt of the palace
claims.note: Wikipedia: the fountain by Alajos Stróbl decorates the western forecourt of the palace.

corrections.find: Its post-war reconstruction, carried out from 1952 to 1966 in a simplified Baroque style, gave the building the outline and the dome you see today, and the medieval fortifications were rebuilt as well.
corrections.replace: Its post-war reconstruction, externally complete by 1966 although the interiors were finished only in the 1980s, took a simplified Baroque form and gave the building the outline and the dome you see today. Some medieval rooms were also uncovered and reconstructed.
corrections.reason: Wikipedia says the palace was rebuilt by 1966 with interiors ready in the 1980s; no source seen for 1952 or for rebuilt medieval fortifications; sources mention medieval rooms unearthed and reconstructed in the 1950s-60s.

corrections.find: The Castle District grew around the medieval royal residence of Buda and the fortified streets above the Danube.
corrections.replace: The Castle District began as a walled town on Castle Hill, founded by King Béla IV after the Mongol invasion of 1241–42, and the royal court soon settled in the growing town.
corrections.reason: Source says the fortified town was founded first and later accommodated the royal court; the old wording implied the reverse and was not stated by any source.

sourceIssues.issue: Returned only a title when fetched; not usable as evidence.
Supports courtyards, streets, churches and viewpoints but not the statement that the district grew around the medieval royal residence.

Lists attractions only; it has no general history of the district, so it does not support historical statements about the district's origin. The Academy page (budavar.abtk.hu) or Wikipedia Várhegy fits that claim better.
Fetch returned only the page title with no body text, so it could not be used to verify anything.

attractions.phase18: The claim that the district 'grew around the royal residence' was not supported and is actually backwards: the Academy's Buda history page says the fortified town was founded first and the royal court was later accommodated in the growing town. attractions.summary: Most facts verified, but the royal box statue location, the details of the 2017-2022 restoration, and one unsourced history sentence were corrected or removed. Phase 18: The staircase remark is supported by Wikipedia (not by the We Love Budapest article it was linked to) and is now attributed and worded as the source words it. The removed 'shared stages' statement is partly supported for opera only (not ballet), so a narrower version was restored in the history section.

claims.claim: Neo-Renaissance by Miklós Ybl, begun 1875, funded by city and Franz Joseph, opened 27 September 1884 as Hungarian Royal Opera House
claims.note: Matches; opera.hu confirms the permit in 1875 and 1884 opening.

claims.claim: Podmaniczky called the tender in 1873 and Ybl won
claims.note: We Love Budapest says so; opera.hu says six architects were invited in 1873 and the jury chose Ybl. The dossier attributes it to 'one account'.

claims.claim: Erkel and Liszt statues by Stróbl; Erkel composed the anthem and was first music director
claims.note: Matches.

claims.claim: Lotz's two Carrara marble sphinxes; original facade sculptures mouldy, replaced in the 1960s
claims.note: Matches.

claims.claim: Auditorium seats about 1,261; three-tonne bronze chandelier by craftsmen from Mainz; Lotz Olympus fresco; Székely and Than muses
claims.note: 1,261, chandelier 3050 kg, Lotz fresco, nine Muses confirmed; opera.hu says 'the chandelier is from Mainz'.

claims.claim: Royal box carries sculptures of the four operatic voices
claims.note: Wikipedia says the royal box is decorated with statues of the four voices, but the Opera's own site (seen in search results) places them in the boxes beside the royal box.

claims.claim: Former smoking room portrait gallery of about 600 backstage workers and musicians; painters paid a beer each (rumour)
claims.note: 'reportedly' paid a beer; worded as rumour.

claims.claim: Hydraulic stage device; electric lighting from 1895; Mahler director 1888-1891; Klemperer 1947-1950
claims.note: Hydraulics and 1895 lighting from We Love Budapest; Mahler and Klemperer dates from Wikipedia.

claims.claim: 1980-1984 renovation reopened 27 Sept 1984; second restoration reopened 12 March 2022
claims.note: Matches.

claims.claim: Second restoration: nearly five seasons, uncovered original wall colours and materials, renewed pipework and structure, connected orchestra pit to auditorium, new stage machinery
claims.note: Budapest Times: 'nearly five seasons'; gold paint restored, marble doorframes and columns returned to original look, basement waterproofing improved, old gas-line cabling issue, orchestra pit rebuilt and made mobile for acoustics, 1984 stage machinery replaced. It does not say the pit was connected to the auditorium.

claims.claim: Erkel Theatre opened 1911 as Népopera, part of the Opera since 1951
claims.note: Matches.

claims.claim: Opening day 1884: spectators pushed past guards
claims.note: Crowd 'overran the security guards'.

claims.claim: History: building brought opera and ballet into a purpose-built theatre after years of sharing stages with drama
claims.note: No source seen for this statement; removed.

resolution.note: The Opera's own page says the National Theatre was increasingly unable to stage drama while also meeting the needs of opera, and that a dedicated opera building was the goal; Wikipedia confirms opera was performed at the National Theatre and moved into the new house on completion. Nothing says ballet shared stages with drama, so ballet is left out and only the opera statement is restored (in the history section, replacing the earlier removal in the long form).

claims.claim: A sweeping staircase was designed so audiences could show off their gowns
claims.note: Not seen on any page opened; stylistic remark, kept but flagged.

resolution.note: Wikipedia: 'A vast, sweeping staircase was an important element of the opera house as it allowed ladies to show off their new gowns.' The linked We Love Budapest article only mentions grand staircases and nothing about gowns; opera.hu does not mention it either. Wording tightened to the source ('ladies', 'new gowns') and attributed to Wikipedia.

claims.claim: Address Andrássy út 22; coordinates 47.50291, 19.05831
claims.note: Wikipedia 47.5028, 19.0581; within ~25 m.

claims.claim: Coordinates 47.50291, 19.05831 and address Andrássy Avenue 22
claims.note: Wikipedia gives 47.50278, 19.05806 and Andrássy Ave 22; about 25 m apart.

claims.claim: Interior includes the main staircase decorated by leading Hungarian artists of the time
claims.note: We Love Budapest: the main staircase, buffet and Red Salon were decorated by the most talented Hungarian artists.

claims.claim: Opera was performed at the National Theatre before 1884 and moved into the new house on completion
claims.note: Wikipedia: 'Upon its completion, the opera section moved into the Hungarian Royal Opera House.'

corrections.find: and the royal box carries sculptures representing the four operatic voices
corrections.replace: and the boxes beside the royal box carry sculptures representing the four operatic voices
corrections.reason: The Opera's own site places the four voice statues in the boxes neighbouring the royal box rather than in the royal box itself.

corrections.find: uncovered original wall colours and materials, renewed pipework and structure, connected the orchestra pit to the auditorium and installed new stage machinery

corrections.find: The building brought opera and ballet into a purpose-built theatre after years of sharing stages with drama.
corrections.reason: No source found for this statement about prior shared stages; the sentence is removed and the remaining paragraph stays grammatical.

corrections.find: A sweeping main staircase was designed to let audiences show off their gowns.

corrections.reason: Wikipedia is the only source found for this; wording tightened to match it and attributed.

claims.note: Matches.

claims.note: Stockhausen concept confirmed; 'hologram-like' appears in other coverage of the dome (search results).

claims.note: Matches; Archinect also gives the 1957-1993 pop exhibition.

claims.note: Gál Éva, Margaret Island (Our Budapest, 2000), via search result: monks and nuns left not later than the conquest of Buda; island deserted by mid-16th century. Seen only as search snippet.

resolution.note: Museum's own article by Domokos Zsuzsanna (opened and text-extracted): the composing desk was made by Liszt's Viennese friend Ludwig Bösendorfer, finished at the turn of 1876-77 and given as a gift (Liszt's letter of 30 Jan 1877); a walnut desk standing in the corner of the study-bedroom, with three drawers above, where 'a kihúzható billentyűs hangszer' (pull-out keyboard instrument, three octaves, quiet metal-plate sound) replaces the middle drawer. It served to check a few runs and fingerings; Liszt composed in his head. So 'in the middle' is correct in the sense of the middle drawer, 'built into the middle for composing' was loose. Rewritten to the museum's wording. Confirmed by https://www.museum.hu/exhibition/11459/The_flat_of_Ferenc_Liszt (gift from the Bösendorfer piano maker, hides a small three-octave keyboard) and the We Love Budapest article (keyboard in the middle of the desk).

attractions.summary: All checked history claims (parish, Gothic church and tower, Ottoman use, Franciscans, 1792 coronation, 1817, 1920, 1945 damage, 1950 demolition, 2025 closure) match the Castle District heritage site, Daily News Hungary and Xpatloop; address and coordinates fit.

claims.note: Matches heritage site.

claims.note: Matches.

claims.note: Matches.

claims.claim: Matthias Church served the German community, Magdalene church the Hungarians

claims.claim: Address

claims.claim: Thermal baths used on site since at least the 12th century, by the Knights Hospitaller
claims.note: Stated; also on Budapest Info page and Budappest.

claims.claim: Wall inside the bath is a remnant of the Ottoman Császár powder mill using spring water as power
claims.note: Stated.

claims.claim: Present complex dates mainly from the 1880s / 'the present bath dates from the mid-1880s'
claims.note: Sources show a longer development: Palotay bought it 1884, joint-stock company 1893 (complex opened 1895), Hikisch's 1921 redesign gave the current form (Budappest: main building completed 1921). Wording softened.

claims.claim: Palotay bought area from treasury in 1884 and named it Szent Lukács; limited company 1893 with mud bath, spa hotel, public steam bath

claims.claim: Rezső Ray the elder designed the hotel; Rezső Hikisch unified facade in Classicist-Biedermeier style in the 1920s
claims.note: Mandadb credits Rezső Ray Sr. with the hotel and Hikisch with the 1920s facade; Hungarian Wikipedia has Hikisch 1921.

claims.claim: Drinking-cure hall 1937 during First International Congress of Bathing
claims.note: Stated; 1937 also in Wikipedia and Budapest Info.

claims.claim: Until Széchenyi and Gellért opened it was Budapest's most significant thermal bath
claims.note: Stated.

claims.claim: Kodály regular guest; Illyés, Déry, Makk, Bacsó notable patrons

claims.claim: Gratitude plaques; many destroyed in WWII, survivors built into walls during renovation
claims.note: Stated (page does not mention 'courtyard' specifically).

claims.claim: Hospital moved into former hotel after the war; National Institute of Rheumatology since 1951

claims.claim: 2013 restoration reported to have received an ICOMOS award
claims.note: Stated (also Hungarian Wikipedia).

claims.claim: Malom Lake 'Turkish bath' was a people's steam bath built by Palotay
claims.note: Stated.

claims.claim: Drinking-water hall 1937, health clinic 1979, first spa hotel 1880s; Császár bath oldest continuously operating (Szokoli Mustafa, Hild 1844)
claims.note: All stated by Wikipedia and Budapest Info.

resolution.note: The Zsigmond tér/M2 walking claim is unsupported and stays removed. The official Lukács site lists buses 9 and 109, trams 4, 6, 17 and 19, and the HÉV (stop Margit híd) as public transport. The tip now quotes that instead of the neighbouring bath's directions.

Phase 18: Builder (Sokollu Mustafa) is supported by the Hospitaller order's own page, a Hungarian local-history page and, with a hedge ('probably'), Hungarian Wikipedia; the year genuinely differs (1574-75 chronogram per the order vs 1570-1572 per Budapest100), and the 1686 survival still rests on tourism sources only. resolution.note: The Hospitaller order's history page: 'Szokollu Musztafa, Buda leghíresebb pasája (1566-78) ekkor fejezte be a hódoltság legszebben megépített fürdőjét' and 'a megfejthető évszám, ami a Veli bej fürdőre vonatkozik, a következő: 1574-75'. Budapest100 (https://budapest100.hu/house/frankel-leo-ut-31-33/) says Sokollu Mustafa built it, completed 1570-1572. Budapest by Locals and Hungary Unlocked repeat 1574-75 and 'survived the recapture of Buda in 1686'; the 1686 point is not on the order's page, so it stays attributed to Budapest by Locals. Description softened to 'of the 1570s' and the alternative date added.

resolution.note: Order's page: Marczibanyi Istvan, who had bought the Csaszarfurdo in 1802, gave the restored complex to the order in 1806 (plaque 'Az apolatlan betegeknek szenteltetett 1806'). Budapest100: he bought it in 1806 and passed on the operating right on condition the profits fund care of Buda's sick. hu.wikipedia also says Marczibanyi (given as Karoly there) bought it in 1806. The year 1806 is solid; 'became the property of the order' is not what both sources say, so the wording now says he handed it to the order and notes the sources' difference.

Existing wording already attributes year and survival and names the alternative date, so it is left unchanged.

attractions.summary: Ganz history, demolition, opening, Europa Nostra award, exhibitions, address and Building E are confirmed; the Széllkapu views over the Castle District and Buda hills could not be confirmed from any page I could open. Phase 18: The Széllkapu view claim is stated verbatim by the official Millenáris about-us page, so it is kept but now attributed to the official site and worded as 'towards' (not 'over'), because no independent source lists the landmarks. The address field held only a name and now has the official street address; coordinates are confirmed. Phase 18: The view claim is stated verbatim by the official Millenáris about-us page ('views towards Margit körút, the Castle District, and the Buda Hills'), and Hungarian press from the 2020 Széllkapu opening (economx.hu) repeats the same phrasing; no independent source (architects' page, OSM, guidebook) confirms the sight lines, so it stays attributed and qualified with no text change. Address, coordinates and several history claims were re-checked and hold.

resolution.note: Infostart, 29 March 2014: three exhibitions open with the renovated Várkert Bazár in 'az épületegyüttes déli palotáiban' (the southern palaces), including the Budapest History Museum's 'Ostromok és hétköznapok' presenting archaeological finds from the site (jewellery, silver coins, vessels, tools, carved stones, a stove reconstruction, Ottoman-period weapon finds). The official site (varkertbazar.hu, exhibitions page /en/kiallitas) currently lists only an outdoor retrospective (Soul Stones, 2025, in the Neo-Renaissance Garden) and no finds display, and its history page does not mention southern palaces; so whether finds are on show today is not confirmed, which the sentence already says. Phase 18: An independent Hungarian source (HVG) confirms the zero point was once at the Royal Palace threshold and was moved near the newly opened Chain Bridge; the 1849 date still comes only from English Wikipedia (tagged for missing citations) and sites copying it, so the text now attributes the date to Wikipedia and the move to HVG. resolution.note: Közterkép: the three figures (Francis of Assisi, Daruma, Gandhi) were stolen in 2007 and recast in Japan in August 2009; the work was unveiled again in 2010. A Fővárosi blog (fovarosi.blog.hu, 2010) says the mould was provided by the widow Akiyama Chiyo and that the replacements were paid for by the Budapest and Buda Castle district municipalities, with the eight figures photographed together in July 2010. A 2020 blog (mrfoster.blog.hu) also says all three were recast in Japan and reinstalled in 2010. XpatLoop 2023 and budappest.com list all eight figures as present. Not stated in sources: exact re-unveiling date (Közterkép says 17 June 2010, the blog only July 2010), so the text says 'by 2010'.

claims.claim: Current use: synagogue, museum and concert hall after 2021 reopening
claims.note: CJA: use is synagogue, museum and concert hall, open to the public in 2021. English Wikipedia: 'Since 2021, the building has also been used as a concert hall and Jewish museum.' Hungarian Wikipedia: can still serve ritual purposes, also concerts, cultural events and conferences. Budapest100: reopened in 2021 for tourists, concerts, performances, events, museum and religious life. The site's text does not claim it is currently open at set times.

claims.claim: Designed by Otto Wagner, consecrated 1872; octagonal prayer hall, neo-Moorish, brick
claims.note: CJA: Otto Wagner, Neo-Moorish, brick, octagonal prayer hall, built 1872. Budapest100 gives construction 1870-1874 and handover in 1874; this is a minor difference in framing (consecration vs. handover) and the site already says sources differ on start dates.

claims.claim: Interior: eight slender iron columns with Alhambra-style capitals; gold, blue and red wall reliefs
claims.note: Hungarian Wikipedia: 'nyolc karcsú vasoszlop' with 'Alhambra oszlopfőkkel' and reliefs in 'arany, kék és vörös színű'. A guide snippet also describes red, blue and gold Alhambra-inspired interior decoration.

claims.claim: Homage to the Dome of the Rock, not an exact replica
claims.note: English Wikipedia: 'as an homage to the style of the octagonal, domed Dome of the Rock shrine in Jerusalem', not an exact replica.

claims.claim: After decades of decay it was restored and reopened in 2021, and sources describe it as serving as a synagogue, a museum and a concert hall.
claims.note: Phase 19: no current official source reachable. Statement is attributed to "sources". A 2026 ticket-seller page shows visitor opening in 2026 and says hours can change because of use as a concert venue; official site not reached. Wording is safe as

resolution.note: Official site: 'a zsinagóga 2021-ben újra megnyílt'; 'Hagyományos funkciója mellett az épület közösségi térként ma koncerteknek, előadásoknak, rendezvényeknek is helyet ad, és a Zsidó Múzeum és Levéltár külső kiállítótereként is szolgál.' CJA (https://cja.huji.ac.il/mhs/browser.php?id=24867&mode=set): 'In 2021, the synagogue was open to the public. It serves as a synagogue, museum, and concert hall.' Text tightened to the official wording (no change in meaning); no opening hours or ticket details were found on the official site, so none are stated.

claims.claim: Built for the Status Quo Ante community / traditionalist Jews
claims.note: Official site: built by the 'neológ' community 'with fittings suited to traditional liturgy'. CJA: Status Quo Ante community. English Wikipedia: built for the Status Quo congregation, meant to serve the Neolog community of Pest, home of the more conservative fraction. Hungarian Wikipedia: built for traditionalists, under Status Quo Ante management from the time of construction. The paragraph now says it was built for traditionalist Jews of the Status Quo Ante, while the official site credits the Neolog community.

claims.claim: Address Rumbach Sebestyén utca 11–13, 1074
claims.note: Official site: '1074 Budapest, Rumbach Sebestyén utca 11-13'; CJA: Rumbach Sebestyén St. 11-13 (OSM uses postcode 1075 for the building, the official site 1074; kept official).
OSM way 259555819 (Rumbach utcai zsinagóga, wikidata Q569083) centre 47.4979011, 19.0589118, about 22 m from the pin.

claims.claim: Designed by Otto Wagner, consecrated 1872, reopened 10 June 2021
claims.note: CJA: erected 1872 by Otto Wagner, reconstruction 2017-2021. The official site says the synagogue was handed over in 1873 ('1873-ben átadott') and built to Otto Wagner's plans; OSM start_date 1873-05-01, consistent with the use permit in May 1873 already in the text. The exact 10 June 2021 date was not re-found on the official site.

claims.claim: Third-party visiting information (open Sunday-Friday, head covering for men)
claims.note: Not stated on the official front page; the site links a news post 'Látogatható a Rumbach Sebestyén utcai zsinagóga' without details. The site text correctly sends visitors to current official information and makes no hours claim.

corrections.find: and they are topped with lotus carvings and small domed towers that resemble minarets.
corrections.replace: and, according to Hungarian Wikipedia, they are topped with lotus-flower carvings and continue in small domed towers that resemble minarets.
corrections.reason: Lotus carvings are only found in Hungarian Wikipedia; attribute rather than state as established fact.

corrections.find: The plaster is greyish-yellow with red brick stripes and blue enamelled bricks.
corrections.replace: Sources describe the colours of the restored facade differently, so the exact palette is left unstated here; according to Hungarian Wikipedia, its central part carries the two tablets of Moses.
corrections.reason: Colour details come from a single lineage (Hungarian Wikipedia) and conflict with other descriptions; removed rather than stated (editor decision in Phase 18). The tablets of Moses detail is attributed.

corrections.find: and sources describe it as serving as a synagogue, a museum and a concert hall.
corrections.replace: and, according to its official site, it is still a synagogue that also hosts concerts and events and serves as an exhibition space of the Jewish Museum and Archives.
corrections.reason: Official site describes current use more precisely than 'sources describe'.

corrections.find: The Center for Jewish Art records that in 2021 the building was open to the public and serving as a synagogue, museum and concert hall.
corrections.replace: The building's official site says it is still a synagogue, that it also hosts concerts, lectures and events, and that it serves as an external exhibition space of the Jewish Museum and Archives; the Center for Jewish Art likewise records that in 2021 it was open to the public as a synagogue, museum and concert hall.
corrections.reason: Adds the official statement alongside the CJA record.

corrections.find: It was built for the Status Quo Ante community, the more traditionalist congregation formed around the 1869 schism in Hungarian Jewry, and the Center for Jewish Art records Otto Wagner, then an emerging Viennese architect, as its designer.
corrections.replace: It was built for traditionalist Jews of the Status Quo Ante community, the congregation formed around the 1869 schism in Hungarian Jewry, although the building's official site says the Neolog community commissioned it with fittings suited to traditional liturgy. The Center for Jewish Art records Otto Wagner, then an emerging Viennese architect, as its designer.
corrections.reason: The official site's attribution differs from CJA and Wikipedia; both are now shown.

sourceIssues.issue: Does not contain the facade colour, lotus, Jachin/Boaz or Alhambra-capital details; it supports only the Dome of the Rock homage, brick material, address and use since 2021.

Supports architect, style, brick, octagonal plan, address and current use, but gives no facade colour or ornament detail. It is also used as sourceUrl for the 'visitor information' history source, which it is not (the label is misleading).
Reachable and supports the 2021 use claim, but dates the building 1872 and does not give a record date; the official site should be added as a source (https://rumbachzsinagoga.hu).

attractions.phase18: Current use is confirmed by the building's own site (rumbachzsinagoga.hu: it is still a synagogue, hosts concerts, lectures and events, serves as an external exhibition space of the Jewish Museum and Archives, and 'reopened in 2021'), plus the Center for Jewish Art record. The description and paragraph now use the official wording. The same official site says the Neolog community commissioned the building, which differs from the Status Quo Ante attribution used in the text (Wikipedia, CJA), so that sentence is now worded to show both.

attractions.summary: Main facts are well supported, but the 1913 facade change is described as plainer in Hungarian Wikipedia and as more ornate in English Wikipedia, so it was qualified; a currency amount (650,000 korona) was removed. Phase 18: Coordinates were missing and are supplied from OSM and Hungarian Wikipedia (about 30 m apart). The house number remains unsettled between sources (29-31 in en/hu Wikipedia, 27-29 at WeLoveBudapest, OSM shows 23-27 for the neighbouring ELTE building), and the official site could not be reached, so the address stays without a number as the text already says. Phase 18: House number resolved: the congregation (MAOIH) states 'Cím: 1075 Budapest, Kazinczy utca 29–31', matching hu.wikipedia, en.wikipedia and BKK; 27-29 appears only on visitor-guide sites. Address field and the hedging sentence are corrected; the existing pin (47.49857, 19.06246) is confirmed against the OSM building centre (47.49857, 19.06245) and sits about 30 m from Wikipedia/Wikidata's rounded 47.4983, 19.0625.

claims.claim: Built 1912-1913 by Sándor and Béla Löffler in Art Nouveau/Secession style influenced by Lechner and late Viennese Secession
claims.note: hu.wikipedia: built 1912-13, Secession, Lechner and late Viennese Secession; en.wikipedia: Art Nouveau, Löfflers.

claims.note: Wikipedia and Budappest say 29-31; WeLoveBudapest says 27-29.

claims.claim: Pest Jewry divided into Neolog, Status Quo Ante and Orthodox
claims.note: Search results from en.wikipedia and others: the 1868-69 Congress led to Orthodox, Neolog and Status Quo camps.

claims.claim: Competition 25 June 1909; jury favoured another design; May 1910 congregation chose Löfflers; plans approved 8 Nov 1910
claims.note: hu.wikipedia confirms these, with Porgesz and Skultetzky as jury choice (spelled Skutetzky in the page).

claims.claim: Budget of 650,000 korona
claims.note: Supported by hu.wikipedia but removed because site rules forbid currency amounts.

claims.claim: School and community headquarters done 1911, handed over 1912; synagogue work began spring 1912; use permit 29 Sept 1913
claims.note: hu.wikipedia and en.wikipedia agree.

claims.claim: July 1913 the architects submitted a plainer facade to cut costs
claims.note: hu.wikipedia says plainer facade with lower material costs; en.wikipedia says the 1913 change gave a more ornate main facade. Sources conflict, so the claim is qualified.

claims.claim: Wrought-iron main gate flanked by two smaller entrances; coloured artificial stone; two-line Hebrew inscription from Genesis 28:17
claims.note: en.wikipedia states each; hu.wikipedia also confirms inscription.

claims.claim: Women's galleries, central reading platform, carved ark, Transylvanian wood-carving motifs, Zsolnay inlays on eastern-wall columns, Miksa Róth windows, over 1,000 seats
claims.note: Budappest: Transylvanian carving, Zsolnay inlays on eastern wall columns, over 1,000 seats; en.wikipedia/WeLoveBudapest: Róth windows; hu.wikipedia: two-level women's galleries, carved ark.

claims.claim: 1944-45 inside ghetto; war damage; restored after 1945; main synagogue later unsafe; congregation used ground floor of neighbouring teacher-training college (now ELTE) and a small prayer house by Sándor Bokor
claims.note: hu.wikipedia confirms all; 'west corner' placement was not separately seen.

claims.claim: Mikveh operated from 1928, reopened 2004 after donation-funded renovation
claims.note: hu.wikipedia and en.wikipedia agree; WeLoveBudapest also mentions the 2004 renovation.

claims.claim: Main synagogue can be visited per hu.wikipedia; other source mentions renovation/fundraising
claims.note: hu.wikipedia: visitable; en.wikipedia: facade repairs and fundraising project. Text is already worded as possibly changed, with no prices.

claims.claim: Metro M2 to Astoria or M4 to Rákóczi tér
claims.note: Budappest gives exactly these directions.

claims.claim: Neo-Gothic synagogue by Sándor Fellner; foundation stone 1887, completed 1888, consecrated 8 August 1888; replaced a ~100-year-old synagogue
claims.note: hu.wikipedia states all of this; en.wikipedia also gives 1888 and Fellner.

claims.claim: Former name Újlak Synagogue; present name Frankel Leó Street Synagogue; in II district, Buda
claims.note: hu.wikipedia: 'Újlaki zsinagóga' former name, II district. OSM places the address in Újlak.

claims.claim: Originally freestanding with entrance on Zsigmond utca among single-storey houses, kosher butcher, community flats; ~21.5 x 19 m; about 400 worshippers
claims.note: hu.wikipedia: entrance on Zsigmond utca, houses, kosher butcher, flats; about 21.5 m by 19 m; built for 400.

claims.claim: 1920s residential building handed over 1 Aug 1928, by Dezső Jakab and son-in-law Aladár Sós, at initiative of former president Berthold Beer; synagogue rebuilt with reinforced concrete slabs and joined to it

claims.claim: Three-bay clinker-brick facade, stepped gables, pointed windows, wooden bimah, two menorahs, ark with Star of David and Tablets, three women's galleries on triple cross vaults, marble plaques
claims.note: hu.wikipedia states these; en.wikipedia confirms the stepped gable.

claims.claim: Used as a stable at the end of WWII; residents deported 1944; black marble plaque 2014; survived siege almost intact; prayer house under socialism; renovated 2000
claims.note: hu.wikipedia: stable at the end of WWII, deported residents, black marble plaque for the 70th anniversary (2014), survived siege nearly undamaged, prayer house under socialism, renovated 2000.

claims.note: hu.wikipedia: Neolog, Ashkenazi rite, Budai Zsidó Hitközség, rabbi Verő Tamás; frankel.hu lists prayer times, contacts and Rabbi Verő Tamás (no clock times quoted in the text).
